# Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks

Che Zhang^(\*) Affiliation:  School of Software & Microelectronics,
Peking University Email: [chengchenghan@stu.ecnu.edu.cn](mailto:)   
Zhenyang Xiao^(\*) Affiliation:  School of Software & Microelectronics,
Peking University Email: [lianyixin@xiaobing.ai](mailto:)    Chengcheng
Han Affiliation: School of Data Science and Engineering, East China
Normal University    Yixin Lian Affiliation: Xiaobing.AI{mmt,
kjn}@stu.pku.edu.cn, fangyj@ss.pku.edu.cn    Yuejian Fang Affiliation: 
School of Software & Microelectronics, Peking University

###### Abstract

Self-correction has achieved impressive results in enhancing the style
and security of the generated output from large language models (LLMs).
However, recent studies suggest that self-correction might be limited or
even counterproductive in reasoning tasks due to LLMs’ difficulties in
identifying logical mistakes.

In this paper, we aim to enhance the self-checking capabilities of LLMs
by constructing training data for checking tasks. Specifically, we apply
the Chain of Thought (CoT) methodology to self-checking tasks, utilizing
fine-grained step-level analyses and explanations to assess the
correctness of reasoning paths. We propose a specialized checking format
called “Step CoT Check”. Following this format, we construct a
checking-correction dataset that includes detailed step-by-step analysis
and checking. Then we fine-tune LLMs to enhance their error detection
and correction abilities.

Our experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning with the “Step CoT Check”
format significantly improves the self-checking and self-correction
abilities of LLMs across multiple benchmarks. This approach outperforms
other formats, especially in locating the incorrect position, with
greater benefits observed in larger models.

For reproducibility, all the datasets and code are provided in
[https://github.com/bammt/Learn-to-check](https://github.com/bammt/Learn-to-check).

## 1 Introduction

The colossal number of parameters and extensive training data of Large
Language Models (LLMs) have led to remarkable performances in reasoning
tasks [Yao et al. (2023b)](#bib.bib35); [Wei et al. (2023)](#bib.bib31),
notably in mathematical problem-solving [Luo et al. (2023)](#bib.bib14);
[Wang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib29); [Yu et al. (2023)](#bib.bib36); [Yuan
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib37). Despite these advancements, there remains
considerable potential to further enhance the mathematical reasoning
capabilities of LLMs.

To further improve the mathematical reasoning capabilities of LLMs, some
studies [Madaan et al. (2023)](#bib.bib15); [Weng et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib33); [Huang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib9); [Saunders et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib22); [Welleck et al. (2022)](#bib.bib32); [Miao et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib16); [Chen et al. (2023)](#bib.bib3) have attempted to
prompt LLMs to identify and self-correct errors in their reasoning
paths, thereby achieving higher accuracy. In general, self-correction
involves two distinct processes: self-checking feedback gathering and
feedback-driven reasoning. The former requires LLMs to review their
previous output and attempt to identify errors within it, while the
latter allows the model to modify and optimize its previous outputs
based on the received feedback.

However, recent research [Huang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib9); [Stechly
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib24); [Valmeekam et al. (2023)](#bib.bib28)
indicates that without external feedback, such as ground truth labels
for determining the stopping point [Shinn et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23);
[Kim et al. (2023)](#bib.bib11), LLMs cannot improve their reasoning
abilities through intrinsic self-correction. This difficulty arises
because LLMs often fail to accurately identify errors in reasoning paths
and provide precise feedback. [Stechly et al. (2023)](#bib.bib24); [An
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib1); [Madaan et al. (2023)](#bib.bib15). This is
counterintuitive because, for humans, verifying whether an answer is
correct is often easier than directly solving the problem. The former is
an NP-hard problem, while the latter is a P problem. Therefore, we
hypothesize that by constructing specific task training, LLMs can
enhance their ability to directly check for errors.

Given these challenges, our work aims to address the limitations by
constructing a checking-correction dataset and then fine-tuning LLMs
using this dateset. For generating the dataset, we first collect
reasoning paths that contain errors and then we propose a specialized
prompt format for checking called “Step CoT Check”. This format involves
evaluating the correctness of each step by sequentially checking
different types of errors and providing detailed explanations. If an
error is detected, the model concludes the check for that step and
provides a summary. Following this format, we generated data to check
erroneous reasoning paths, and subsequently used these checks to create
a correction dataset. Then we fine-tune our models on a mixed dataset of
CoT data and checking-correction data.

In our setup, the entire reasoning process includes a stage of direct
reasoning and two stages of self-correction: (1) direct reasoning, (2)
self-checking feedback gathering and (3) feedback-driven reasoning. Our
training data encompasses three different tasks, each corresponding to
one of these stages. And in the stage 2, we compared the performance of
the Step CoT Check format with two other prompt formats: All Direct
Check and Step Direct Check.

Our contributions are threefold:

1.  1.  We propose using training data specifically designed to check
        reasoning paths and demonstrate their effectiveness in enhancing the
        self-checking capabilities. This approach enables LLMs to achieve
        self-correction independently of external data.
2.  2.  We introduce a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) method that incorporates
        checking tasks. Specifically, we propose the “Step CoT Check” format
        for checking mathematical reasoning tasks, which categorizes error
        types and elucidates the reasoning process prior to judgment,
        thereby improving interpretability. This approach markedly surpasses
        traditional direct answer verification techniques.
3.  3.  We have released a checking-correction dataset to improve the
        performance of LLMs on reasoning tasks. To our knowledge, this
        dataset is the first to use fine-grained, step-by-step explanations
        to annotate errors in LLMs’ outputs.

## 2 Related Work

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, initially pioneered by [Wei et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib31), has significantly advanced the reasoning
capabilities of large language models (LLMs). This approach, which
enhances LLMs by incorporating detailed reasoning steps into few-shot
examples, has been foundational in improving performance across various
reasoning tasks. Subsequent research has expanded upon this, introducing
methodologies like Self-Consistency [Wang et al. (2022)](#bib.bib30),
various prompting techniques [Zhou et al. (2022)](#bib.bib38); [Drozdov
et al. (2022)](#bib.bib5), Self-Training [Huang et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib8), Verifier [Li et al. (2022)](#bib.bib13), Tree of
Thought [Yao et al. (2023a)](#bib.bib34) and DialCoT [Han et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib7). The effectiveness of CoT has been demonstrated in
domains including logical, commonsense, and mathematical reasoning.
Despite the success, these models are not without their flaws. They are
still prone to reasoning confusion, generating hallucinations, and
computational errors. A prevailing strategy to rectify these undesired
behaviors of LLMs is learning from feedback. Extensive research [Huang
et al. (2022)](#bib.bib8); [Madaan et al. (2023)](#bib.bib15); [Gero
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib6); [Jiang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib10) has been
undertaken to improve LLMs through the paradigm of learning from
feedback. However, [Huang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib9) found that
self-improvement is not effective when oracle labels are not available.
This may be attributed to the limited capability of LLMs to identify
errors. Previous works have primarily focused on self-correction,
overlooking the enhancement of the models’ error identification
capabilities. This paper addresses the gap by meticulously constructing
training data that includes steps for detecting and correcting errors,
thereby strengthening the model’s capability to identify mistakes.

## 3 Methodology

In this section, we present our methodology, which comprises two
components: checking-correction data generation and fine-tuning LLMs.
The former component involves collecting erroneous reasoning paths,
generating data that includes a detailed checking process and the
revised answers. The latter involves fine-tuning the model on a combined
dataset that contains three tasks: direct reasoning, checking the
correctness of the reasoning paths and pointing out the error locations,
and re-reasoning to obtain the correct answers.

### 3.1 Checking-Correction Data Generation

The process of generating the checking-correction dataset is detailed in
Figure
[1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Checking-Correction Data Generation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks").

![Refer to caption](2402.13035v3/fig_2.png)

Figure 1: The process of checking-correction dataset generation.

#### 3.1.1 Collecting Reasoning Paths with Errors

We use a generator model $`\mathcal{M}_{g}`$ to produce reasoning path
$`P(Ans(P)\neq a`$, and $`a`$ is the correct answer.) for original
question $`Q`$, then we get pairs $`x=(Q,P)`$. Like  [An et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib1), we use a newline character as a delimiter to
decompose $`P`$ into fine-grained reasoning steps
$`s_{1},s_{2},\ldots,s_{K}`$, and append “Step N:” before each step.

To simplify the notation, we use $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$ to represent
the reasoning path with logical errors. For comparison, we use
$`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$ to represent the reasoning paths that
lead to a correct answer.

#### 3.1.2 Error Type Definition

To construct a prompt format suitable for LLMs to check the answers to
mathematical problems, we categorize and analyze the types of errors in
a certain step of the generation $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$ mentioned
above. In mathematical reasoning tasks, the types of errors are as
follows:

1.  1.  Goal Errors: The model outputs the process of calculating a quantity
        that was already mentioned in the known conditions or a quantity
        that could not be computed based on the existing known conditions.
        Alternatively, it calculates an intermediate quantity that is
        irrelevant to the final problem’s solution, ultimately leading to a
        deviation in the reasoning path.
2.  2.  Computational Expression Errors: The model experiences a
        hallucination or misunderstands the given conditions of the problem,
        leading to an incorrect process for calculating an intermediate
        quantity. This often manifests as the outputted computational
        expression not matching the given conditions.
3.  3.  Calculation Errors: The model correctly identifies the intermediate
        quantity that needs to be calculated and outputs the correct
        computational expression, but the calculation result is incorrect.

Figure 2: The reasoning process combined with self-correction. The
Process involves three stages. Stage 1 involves direct reasoning for a
given question. Stage 2 examines the direct reasoning path and provides
feedback at the end. If Stage 2 check identifies errors, Stage 3 is then
initiated. Stage 3 requires the model to generate a new reasoning path
and attempt to correct the erroneous answer given the question, original
answer, and feedback.

#### 3.1.3 Checking Data Generation

For a reasoning path $`P`$ involving $`K`$ steps, we prompt a feedback
model $`\mathcal{M}_{f}`$ to generate checking data for each step
$`s_{k},k\in[1,K]`$ one by one. For each step, $`\mathcal{M}_{f}`$ check
sequentially according to the three types of errors mentioned above and
generate a detailed explanation process.

1.  1.  Reasoning Goal Appropriateness: Assesses whether the computational
        goal of $`s_{k}`$ is conducive to solving the question. If the
        step’s objective is unreasonable or redundant, it is deemed
        incorrect.
2.  2.  Computational Expression Correctness: Identifies the known
        conditions related to $`s_{k}`$’s computational goal and evaluates
        if the computation aligns with the problem statement and whether the
        derived expression achieves the computational goal correctly.
3.  3.  Verification through Inverse Operations: The correctness of the
        computation is checked by performing inverse operations on the
        derived expression.

If the above error types are detected, the model will generate a brief
summary of the error message; otherwise, it will summary that the step
is correct. Since the three types of errors are hierarchical and
subsequent errors may depend on the initial error, it only makes sense
to check for a particular type of error if the previous types have not
occurred. For the same reason, we only generate the checking data of
steps up to the first wrong step.¹¹ 1 In practical experiments,
redundant steps are also considered correct as long as they do not
contain logical errors. Only steps that contain logical errors are used
as stopping criteria. If step $`s_{n},n\in[1,K]`$ is determined to be
incorrect after these checks, a concise summary indicating the error
will be generated and denoted as $`F_{n}`$. We refer to this method of
step-by-step checking of arithmetic reasoning paths with detailed
explanations as “Step CoT Check”.

Before generating data on a large scale, we use
GPT-4-1106-preview [OpenAI et al. (2023)](#bib.bib19) as
$`\mathcal{M}_{f}`$ and manually assess the quality of 50 checking data
samples of $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$ to ensure data quality. Among
these, 43 entries are perfect(accurately identify the erroneous step and
provide precise analysis), while 5 entries are good (pinpoint the
incorrect step but offer analysis that lacks sufficient accuracy). 2
entries are poor (fail to identify the location of the error). Based on
this human evaluation, we suppose the overall quality of check data is
sufficient for fine-tuning.

To ensure that the model can effectively learn and distinguish between
correct and incorrect reasoning processes and reduce bias for the
further fine-tuning stage, in addition to $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$, we
also filter some original answers from the CoT dataset as
$`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$ and generate their checking data. ²² 2
The specific prompts and examples of generated data can be found in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Prompt for Checking-corection Data Generation ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks").

#### 3.1.4 Correction Data Generation

We task a correction model $`\mathcal{M}_{c}`$ to generate correction
data. Specifically, given $`(Q,P,F_{n})`$, where
$`P\in\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$, the model is required to generate a
revised reasoning path $`P_{r}`$. We use regular expressions to compare
$`P_{r}`$ with the original answer $`a`$ to question $`Q`$. If
$`P_{r}`$’s final answer is correct, we then add the checking data and
correction data to the Checking-correction dataset; otherwise, we drop
the data sample. For the $`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$’s checking data,
we also add it to the Checking-correction dataset.

### 3.2 Fine-Tuning LLMs

After generating the checking-correction data, we fine-tune the LLMs to
evaluate whether these models can self correct. To this end, we mainly
compare the performance of two fine-tuning settings:

- •
  Fine-Tuning on CoT Data We fine-tune the model on GSM8K training data
  alone. To facilitate comparison with our method, we only use the
  original train set and don’t generate additional reasoning paths for
  training. We use the model fine-tuned with the original CoT data as a
  baseline and compare it with our self-correction method.
- •
  Fine-Tuning on CoT Data + Checking-Correction data In addition to CoT
  data, we also used the Checking-Correction dataset for training. To
  eliminate the effect of data size, we employed a replacement method,
  substituting one piece of data from the original CoT dataset with the
  corresponding Checking-Correction data for the same question $`Q`$.

The entire reasoning process is illustrated in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1.2 Error Type Definition ‣ 3.1 Checking-Correction Data Generation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks").
And in the stage of Self-Checking Feedback Gathering, we employed three
different prompt formats and compared the performance of the fine-tuned
models:

- •
  All Direct Check: Input the original question and the original
  reasoning path into the model $`\mathcal{M}`$, instructing
  $`\mathcal{M}`$ to check the entire reasoning path. The model should
  directly output the first step that contains a logical error.
- •
  Step Direct Check: In each inference round, input the original
  question and the original reasoning path into the model
  $`\mathcal{M}`$, ask $`\mathcal{M}`$ to check one step
  $`s_{k},k\in[1,K]`$. The complete path $`P`$ is input to provide
  $`\mathcal{M}`$ with a holistic view. The model stop the process as
  soon as it finds $`s_{n}`$ containing an error, then we get the error
  feedback $`F_{n}`$.
- •
  Step CoT Check: The input is the same with “Step Direct Check”. But
  before outputs a checking conclusion for each step, this method
  requires $`\mathcal{M}`$ to analyze step $`s_{k}`$ for correctness
  from three dimensions as mentioned before.

The input-output format of CoT data and correction data used for
fine-tuning are showed in the
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Prompt for Reasoning Combined with Self-correction Mechanisms ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks").
For All Direct Check and Step Direct Check formats, we use regular
expressions and rules to generate their responses.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experiment Step

##### CoT Dataset

Our research focuses on multi-step arithmetic reasoning problems and
employs the GSM8K dataset [Cobbe et al. (2021)](#bib.bib4). GSM8K
contains high quality linguistically diverse grade school math word
problems with 7,473 examples in the training set and 1,319 test cases.

##### Generate the Checking-Correction Dataset

We use LLaMA-7b and LLaMA-13b [Touvron et al. (2023a)](#bib.bib25) as
the generator model $`\mathcal{M}_{g}`$ to generate
$`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$, which is fine-tuned for one epoch on the
GSM8K training set to be able to learn the CoT format. Subsequently, we
increase the temperature of $`\mathcal{M}_{g}`$ and generate five
different responses for each question in the training set. For each
question, we filter one reasoning path that contains an incorrect
answer.

We use GPT-4-1106-preview [OpenAI et al. (2023)](#bib.bib19) as
$`\mathcal{M}_{f}`$ to generate accurate $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$’s
checking data. However, generating $`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$’s
checking data is relatively simple, requiring only the "reading
comprehension" of the problem conditions and each step in the reasoning
path. To save costs, we use GPT-3.5-turbo [OpenAI (2023)](#bib.bib18) as
$`\mathcal{M}_{f}`$ to generate $`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$’s
checking data and as $`\mathcal{M}_{c}`$ to generate correction data.

As a result, There are approximately 4,500 instances of
$`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$’s checking and correction data, and 2,000
instances of $`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$’s checking data in the
checking-correction dataset.

##### Fine-Tuning and Evaluation

We conduct experiment on LLaMA-2 [Touvron et al. (2023b)](#bib.bib26)
models with 7B and 13B parameters, trained on 4 Nvidia A100 80GB GPUs.
The models undergo full parameter fine-tuning, employing a learning rate
of $`8\times 10^{-6}`$, over three epochs, with a cumulative batch size
of 32. For models trained on mixed data, we used mixed data and replaced
the original 4,000 GSM8K entries with checking-correction data. After
extensive experimentation, we determined the optimal ratio of
$`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$ to $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$ for each
checking format. For the “All Direct Check” and “Step Direct Check”
methods, we adopted a ratio of 3000:1000, while for the “Step CoT Check”
method, we chose a ratio of 3700:300. (more information about the data
ratio is showed in
[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Further Analysis on Data Proportion ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks")).

The effectiveness of the checkpoints is evaluate on the GSM8K benchmark
and additional three datasets: MultiArith [Roy and Roth
(2015)](#bib.bib21), ASDiv [Miao et al. (2020)](#bib.bib17), and
SVAMP [Patel et al. (2021)](#bib.bib20). Each dataset contains
elementary mathematical problems with distinct lexical distributions.
Our evaluation strategy validates the robustness of our method across
these varied data distributions. We use the full 1,319-instance GSM8K
set, and randomly sample subsets from MultiArith (400), ASDiv (500), and
SVAMP (500).

Checkpoint evaluations are conducted using the vLLM library [Kwon et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib12). For direct reasoning path generation, we set the
temperature parameter to zero. The check and correction mechanism
employs a temperature of 0.5, complemented by a top-p value of 0.85 and
a top-k setting of 30. For all reasoning tasks, we apply a repetition
penalty of 1.2 [Artiges et al. (2019)](#bib.bib2), which effectively
mitigates the generation of duplicate content.

##### Performance Of Reasoning Combined Self-Correction

![Refer to caption](2402.13035v3/fig_3.png)

Figure 3: Accuracy($`\%`$) of checking the correctness of reasoning
paths obtained by itself.

Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results and Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks")
and
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Performance Of Reasoning Combined Self-Correction ‣ 4.2 Main Results and Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks")
illustrate the performance of models trained using our three prompt
formats on the test sets. When a portion of the CoT data is replaced
with checking-correction instances, there is a decrease in the models’
direct reasoning accuracy. This decrease is more pronounced in the
LLaMA-2-7B model, while it is much smaller in the LLaMA-2-13B model.
This suggests that models with larger parameters may be able to obtain
extra information from the Checking-Correction data, thereby somewhat
improving CoT performance [An et al. (2023)](#bib.bib1).

For each dataset, all models show a significant increase in accuracy
following self-correction. And in almost all datasets, models trained on
mixed data outperform those fine-tuned solely on CoT data. Notably,
compared to the COT baseline, the improvement in the LLaMA-2-13B model
is more significant than in the LLaMA-2-7B model, with the former
showing an average increase of 5.5% and the latter 3.8%. This
discrepancy is primarily due to a larger reduction in direct reasoning
performance in the LLaMA-2-7B model following data substitution. In the
LLaMA-2-13B model, the "Step CoT Check" method significantly outperforms
other checking methodologies, indicating that in models with larger
parameters, categorizing error types and explicitly displaying the
checking process can provide more precise feedback.

$`Step`$ denotes the rate of successfully identifying the first wrong

To fairly evaluate the model’s capability of checking CoT traces and
finding errors, we sampled 200 reasoning traces from GSM8K and manually
annotated the first incorrect step. This sample included 100
$`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$ and 100 $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$. In
addition to our fine-tuned models, we also conducted experiments on the
models without fine-tuning, as well as on two closed-source LLMs:
GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4-1106-preview. When using the few-shot method to
prompt these models, the original model may fail to follow complex
prompts and output incorrect steps. Therefore, we required the model to
directly evaluate the entire reasoning path to determine its
correctness. When generating arithmetic reasoning paths, we find that
the probability of obtaining the correct answer after a logical error
occurs is extremely low. Therefore, when checking the reasoning path
step by step, if any step is deemed incorrect, we mark the entire
reasoning path as incorrect. Only when all steps are correct do we mark
the entire reasoning path as correct.

As shown in Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Comparison of Checking Abilities. ‣ 4.2 Main Results and Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks"),
the original LLaMA models performed poorly in checking, just above
random (50%). Although the performance on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 seems quite
good (with an accuracy of 70% for the former and 89% for the latter), it
is worth noting that in direct reasoning scenarios, the accuracies of
GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are 75.9% and 95% [Tyen et al. (2024)](#bib.bib27),
respectively. If the model’s ability to judge correctness is comparable
to its ability to directly output the correct answer (assuming the
model’s accuracy in judging the correctness of a reasoning path on
questions beyond its capability range is 50%), then the accuracy of
checking should be 89.95% and 97.5%. It is evident that in LLMs that
have not undergone specialized training, the ability to verify a
reasoning path is significantly lower than the ability to directly
output the correct answer to a question. We believe that it is precisely
this "mismatch" between direct reasoning and checking abilities that
leads to ineffective intrinsic self-correction.

In all of our fine-tuned models, the average accuracy exceeds 70%, which
is significantly better than the untrained base models. This indicates
that through training, the models’ self-checking capabilities have been
enhanced. Notably, the LLaMA-2-13B model performs exceptionally well in
the “Step CoT Check” method, achieving an 81.5% accuracy in path
checking and demonstrating a higher success rate in identifying the
initial incorrect step, significantly outperforming other methods.
However, on the LLaMA-2-7B model, although the probability of
identifying the initial incorrect step is relatively high, its accuracy
in checking the path does not show a significant advantage compared to
the other two formats, suggesting that similar to CoT reasoning[Wei
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib31), CoT for checking is also more effective in
models with larger parameters.

Despite the LLaMA-2-7B model’s lower probability of accurately
identifying specific erroneous steps, self-correction still leads to
significant improvements in the previous experiments. This is because,
although the model may not precisely pinpoint the error, it can still
recognize incorrect answers, thus providing numerous incorrect paths
with opportunities for regeneration and subsequent correction.

### 4.3 Ablation Study

To examine the propensity of LLMs to commit specific errors and to
validate the effectiveness of our "Step CoT Check" three-step checking
method, we conducted an ablation study focusing on the “Step CoT Check”
implemented on the LLaMA-2-13B model. The findings are catalogued in
Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks").
Among the 541 error paths correctly detected, 20.1% of the errors were
successfully corrected to be accurate. Calculation errors were the most
common, accounting for approximately 61.1% of the total errors. These
errors usually stem from the LLMs’ inability to correctly understand the
relationships in the problem or the erroneous use of non-existent
conditions, leading to the incorrect construction of mathematical
expressions. These computational missteps proved challenging to rectify,
with a mere 18% being corrected during the third step, signaling an
avenue for future enhancement.

Goal errors, conversely, represent a category of errors more amenable to
correction, with a rectification rate of 24%. Regarding computation,
LLMs were found to be more susceptible to miscalculations when the
equation involved multiple numerical entities or integrated unknowns.

|                         |       |         |           |       |
| ----------------------- | ----- | ------- | --------- | ----- |
|                         | Goal  | Formula | Calculate | Total |
| Number of wrong cases   | 131   | 329     | 81        | 541   |
| Successfully correction | 31    | 61      | 17        | 109   |
| Performance gains       | 1.74% | 3.11%   | 0.99%     | 5.84% |

Table 3: The results of ablation study. In the table, Performance gains
is the proportion of “wrong to correct” minus the number of “correct to
wrong” cases.

### 4.4 Further Analysis on Data Proportion

The experiments in this section use the Step Check prompt, and fine tune
on LLama-2-13B.

| $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}:\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$ | $`\text{{Step}}_{\times}:\text{{Step}}_{\checkmark}`$ | Ratio | Check Accuracy($`\%`$)         |                            |             | Correct Rate($`\%`$) |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----- | ------------------------------ | -------------------------- | ----------- | -------------------- |
|                                                       |                                                       |       | $`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$ | $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$ | $`Average`$ |                      |
| 2000:2000                                             | 2000:9260                                             | 0.22  | 93.6                           | 36.2                       | 60.8        | 45.3                 |
| 3000:1000                                             | 3000:7225                                             | 0.42  | 88.0                           | 47.0                       | 64.5        | 47.5                 |
| 3500:500                                              | 3500:6117                                             | 0.57  | 84.5                           | 61.8                       | 72.2        | 50.3                 |
| 3700:300                                              | 3700:5681                                             | 0.65  | 78.9                           | 75.0                       | 76.8        | 51.2                 |
| 4000:0                                                | 4000:4990                                             | 0.80  | 46.1                           | 88.1                       | 69.2        | 48.6                 |

Table 4: Results of the data scaling experiment. The table displays how
the number of correct and incorrect reasoning paths in the training data
have an effect on the accuracy of the check and the correct rate of the
reasoning combined with self-correction.

##### The check ability has a relationship with the data ratio.

To discern the influence of the proportion of
$`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$ confirmations to
$`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$ corrections within a pool of 4,000 training
data replacements, we adjusted their ratios and documented the outcomes
in Table
[4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.4 Further Analysis on Data Proportion ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks").
On average, a $`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$ comprised 3.33 correct
steps ($`\text{{Step}}_{\checkmark}`$) checking, whereas a
$`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$ included an average of 1.24 correct steps
($`\text{{Step}}_{\checkmark}`$) checking and 1.0 wrong steps
($`\text{{Step}}_{\times}`$) checking. When the ratio of
$`\text{{Step}}_{\checkmark}`$ to $`\text{{Step}}_{\times}`$ is too
high, the model may tend to judge the steps as correct, thereby creating
bias. Conversely, an excess of incorrect-checking data may lead the
model to judge answers as incorrect more frequently, thereby increasing
the instances of "correct becoming wrong," and consequently reducing
performance.

From the table, it can be observed that maintaining a ratio of
approximately 0.65 between $`\text{{Step}}_{\times}`$ and
$`\text{{Step}}_{\checkmark}`$ in the training set allows the model to
achieve a high level of accuracy in distinguishing between correct and
incorrect steps. This equilibrium facilitated the highest performance
enhancement through a single iteration of the self-correction process.

##### More checking-corection data can continuously improve the reasoning capability of LLMs.

Unlike previous experiments, we use the full GSM8K training dataset and
add our own checking-correction data. We aim to see how increasing
checking-correction data affects the model’s reasoning, keeping the
original reasoning data the same. We adhere to the optimal ratio of
$`\text{{Path}}_{\checkmark}`$ and $`\text{{Path}}_{\times}`$
ascertained from preceding experiments. Fig.
[4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ More checking-corection data can continuously improve the reasoning capability of LLMs. ‣ 4.4 Further Analysis on Data Proportion ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Learning to Check: Enhancing Self-Correction Capabilities in Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks")
shows that both direct and self-corrected reasoning improve as we
increase the checking-correction data.

Similar to the insights from LEMA [An et al. (2023)](#bib.bib1), We
found that LLMs can also enhance their direct CoT reasoning abilities by
training on our checking-correction dataset. Additionally, an increased
corpus of checking-correction data markedly bolsters the model’s
self-correction proficiency. Combining reasoning with self-correction
improves faster than direct reasoning alone. These results endorse the
inclusion of error-annotated correction data within the training regimen
of an inference model, positing that an expanded dataset catalyzes
improved inferential processes within the model. Consequently, the
model’s self-corrective capacity is significantly enhanced, culminating
in substantial performance advancements through the mechanism of
self-correction.

Figure 4: Accuracy ($`\%`$) of direct reasoning and reasoning combined
with self-correction on GSM8K as checking-corection data types increase.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we focused on improving the self-correction capabilities
of LLMs by enhancing their self-checking abilities. By conducting an
in-depth analysis of error patterns in mathematical reasoning, we
developed the “Step CoT Check” prompt and constructed a
checking-correction dataset. This dataset, combined with the original
CoT data, has been instrumental in training models that exhibit improved
self-checking and self-correction, reducing dependence on external
feedback or ground truth labels for error identification and correction.
Notably, models fine-tuned with our “Step CoT Check” prompt demonstrated
superior performance over those trained with alternative prompts. This
approach not only enhances the precision of feedback but also
significantly increases correctness rates, showing the effectiveness of
our method in refining LLMs for complex reasoning tasks.

## Limitations

Our paper has some limitations, which we leave for future work:

##### The computational cost of the step level Check

Compared to direct reasoning and checking the whole path at once,
although step-by-step check leads to better performance, it requires
more inference rounds. On the GSM8K dataset, inference using
step-by-step checking combined with correction process requires 4.8
model calls compared to only one for direct reasoning and 2.6 for
checking the whole path at once. In practical use, there is a trade-off
between performance and resource consumption.

##### Lack of applicability to broader reasoning tasks.

We analyze the types of mistakes in mathematical reasoning and propose a
set of hints for checking the reasoning process. Our approach focuses on
checking and correcting errors in mathematical reasoning problems, and
it remains to be investigated in future work how to extend this approach
to a wider range of reasoning tasks.

##### Lack of experimentation on larger data sizes and scale language models.

Due to constraints on computational resources and funding, we do not
conduct experiments on larger scale language models(\>20B), or generate
additional CoT and correction data like other works. Thus the
performance on larger LLMs and sufficient amount of training data
remains undetermined. We will further explore the performance of our
method on larger data sizes and scale language models in future
research.

## Ethics Statement

The proposed method has no obvious potential risks. All the scientific
artifacts used/created are properly cited/licensed, and the usage is
consistent with their intended use. Also, we open up our codes and
hyper-parameters to facilitate future reproduction without repeated
energy cost.
